tagline.text: The first president's residence, where Philippine independence was first declared

best_season.label: Best time to visit
best_season.text: Year-round (dry season, December–May, is most pleasant)

children.text: The residence of Emilio Aguinaldo, the first president, where Philippine independence was declared on June 12, 1898. You can tour the wooden mansion with its secret passages and hidden rooms, the window and balcony where independence was proclaimed, and a museum of revolutionary history, all free of charge — a great half-day history trip near Manila.
Aguinaldo Shrine is the birthplace and residence of Emilio Aguinaldo, standing in the middle of Kawit, Cavite, southwest of Manila. Aguinaldo was born in this house on
March 22, 1869

, led the Philippine Revolution against Spain, and became the first president of the First Philippine Republic. For Filipinos, this is the place where the country first declared independence, a national shrine that appears in every textbook.
On

, Aguinaldo proclaimed independence from Spain from a window on the second floor of this house. That day, the Philippine flag, made in Hong Kong, was officially raised for the first time, and the march that later became the national anthem was played for the first time. The ornate independence balcony now on the facade was added when Aguinaldo extensively renovated the house in
; the declaration itself was originally made from the plain window. This is also why the Philippines marks its independence day on June 12.
Aguinaldo donated the house and grounds to the government on
, and died the following year, on
February 6, 1964

, at age 94; he is buried in a marble tomb in the backyard of the house. That same year, a republic act designated it a national shrine, and it is now managed by the National Historical Commission of the Philippines (NHCP). The ground floor houses a museum of revolutionary history, and the second-floor living room and bedrooms are toured with a guide.

The building itself is a sight to see. The white wooden mansion, topped with a five-story lookout tower, is full of secret passages and hidden rooms once used to hide weapons and documents, a map of the Philippines carved into the ceiling, and furniture engraved with the flag and sun motifs. There's no entrance fee, and it's about an hour's drive from Manila, making it an easy recommendation for travelers interested in Philippine history, families with children, and expats who have just started life in the Philippines.

blocks.title: Take a photo in front of the independence balcony

children.text: The front balcony hung with the flag is the exact scene that appears on Philippine banknotes and in textbooks. Viewed from the reflecting pool in the plaza in front of the house, the tower and balcony fit into a single frame.

blocks.title: Tour the interior of the house with a guide

children.text: You'll be taken in order through the second-floor great hall, the window where independence was proclaimed, Aguinaldo's bedroom and dining room, and the kitchen. The guide shares the story behind each room, so don't hesitate to ask questions.

blocks.title: Find the secret passages and hidden rooms

children.text: True to a revolutionary leader's home, there are spaces behind the furniture and walls once used to hide documents and weapons, and a secret staircase leading to the floor below. Stories of a secret passage said to reach a nearby church are told too, and children especially find them fascinating.

blocks.title: The map of the Philippines and national symbols on the ceiling

children.text: On the ceiling of the second-floor state dining room is a wood-relief map of the Philippines about
7m
long, with only Cavite Bay, the center of the revolution, painted red. It's also fun to hunt for the sun-and-three-stars motif carved into doors and furniture throughout.

The museum, given a modern makeover by the NHCP, lays out the course of the revolution — from the founding of the Katipunan through the Battle of Cavite, the Pact of Biak-na-Bato, and the Philippine-American War — with photos, artifacts, and video. Unexpected domestic touches also survive inside the house, such as the family's old bowling lane and swimming pool.
A marble tomb where Aguinaldo is laid to rest stands in the garden behind the house. It's a quiet spot, so it's best to remove your hat and pay a brief respect.

blocks.title: Aguinaldo Park and the equestrian statue

children.text: The plaza across from the house has an equestrian statue of Aguinaldo holding a sword, a flagpole, and a reflecting pool. It's a good spot for a stroll at dusk when the house lights come on.
In the same town of Kawit, in Binakayan village, about a
10–15-minute
drive away, stands the house museum of Baldomero Aguinaldo, Emilio's cousin and fellow revolutionary. Seeing both gives a fuller picture of Kawit's revolutionary history.

If time allows, stopping at the Las Piñas Bamboo Organ church on the way back to Manila fits naturally into the route. To combine it with Tagaytay, see the shrine in the morning and head south in the afternoon.

From the Parañaque Integrated Terminal Exchange (PITX) or Baclaran, take a bus or jeepney bound for Kawit, Noveleta, or Cavite City and get off in Kawit town (Tirona Highway). Depending on traffic, it takes about
1–2 hours
, for a fare of about
It helps to tell the conductor in advance to let you off at the "Aguinaldo Shrine." If you get off on the main road, take a tricycle the rest of the way to the shrine.
Phase 1 of the LRT-1 Cavite Extension opened in
November 2024
, so from central Manila you can ride the LRT, get off at PITX station, and walk straight to the PITX terminal. The LRT fare is about
(single-journey ticket). The phase 2 and 3 sections, including Niog station near Kawit, are targeting an opening around
, so for now you have to transfer to a bus or jeepney at PITX.
From Makati or Malate, taking the Manila–Cavite Expressway (CAVITEX) covers about
, taking about
40 minutes–1 hour 30 minutes
without traffic. Grab fares run about
one way, and toll fees may add to that.
Grabs back to Manila from Kawit can take a while to find, so if you're in a group, it's more convenient to book a round-trip car.
Enter CAVITEX from Roxas Boulevard, take the Kawit exit, then follow Tirona Highway into town. There's parking around the shrine and the park, but it gets crowded on weekends and holidays.
Roads toward Cavite have heavy rush-hour traffic from
6–9 AM
and
4–8 PM
. Avoiding these windows can cut your travel time nearly in half.
Short trips around Kawit town cost about
by tricycle, or about
to charter one for a special fare. If you want to visit the Baldomero Aguinaldo Shrine as well, agree on a round-trip and waiting fare before you set off.
Visits are mostly indoors, so you can go any time of year, but the drier
December–May
season is most pleasant.
December–February
is relatively cool, comfortable enough for a walk in the park too, while
April–May
can climb to
at midday, so it's best to visit early in the morning.
During the
June–October

rainy season, afternoon showers and typhoons are frequent, and the low-lying areas of Kawit and Bacoor along Manila Bay often flood when it rains hard. Postpone your visit on days with a typhoon warning. Every year on
June 12

, Independence Day, the shrine holds a flag-raising ceremony and celebration that's a great way to feel the atmosphere, but security and the event can limit regular viewing or make it very crowded. Choose a weekday morning for a quieter visit.

Since Aguinaldo Shrine is a day trip from Manila, there's rarely any need to stay overnight. If you're splitting a Cavite history tour over two days or continuing on to Tagaytay, a business hotel in the Bacoor/Imus area (about
per night), close to malls and restaurants, makes for easy onward travel.

Cavite is a coastal province, so seafood cooking is well developed here. Bacoor has long been famous for mussel (tahong) farming, so you can eat mussel soup or buttered garlic mussels cheaply, and Cavite City's signature pancit pusit — noodles stir-fried black with squid ink — is hard to find in other provinces. Rosario's smoked fish tinapa, and Cavite-style caldereta and bacalao are also local specialties. Simple local eateries and bakeries surround the shrine, and for more options, head to the restaurant rows of the Bacoor/Imus malls, about
10–20 minutes
by car.
Opening hours are usually Tuesday to Sunday, roughly
8 AM–4 PM
, closed on Mondays. Hours can change for holidays, events, or repair work, so check the official NHCP page for the latest notices.
The second floor of the house is often toured with a guide in small groups. It's quieter right after opening than after
10 AM
on weekdays, when tour groups tend to arrive.
There's no entrance fee, but if you found the guide's explanation valuable, it's local etiquette to leave something in the donation box near the exit.
Reading a little beforehand about the Pact of Biak-na-Bato, the 1898 declaration of independence, and the course of the Philippine-American War makes the museum exhibits much more rewarding.
Photos of the front balcony are sharpest with morning front lighting. Try shooting the house reflected in the pool from the park side on a windless day.

The old Philippine five-peso bill once featured Aguinaldo's portrait and the scene of the independence declaration at this house. Comparing the illustration with the real place is a good learning activity for children.
Coming from southern Manila, it pairs well with the Las Piñas Bamboo Organ church; heading south from Cavite, it pairs well with Tagaytay.

This is a national shrine and burial site. Don't touch the furniture and artifacts inside the house, and don't take photos where signs prohibit it. Modest dress is recommended instead of sleeveless tops or short shorts.
The shrine is closed on Mondays and some holidays, and part of the house or museum may close during repair work. Check ahead so you don't make the trip for nothing.
Roads toward Cavite see heavy traffic even from Manila. Allow extra time for the return trip, and avoid traveling during the evening rush hour.
After heavy rain in the wet season, low-lying roads in Kawit and Bacoor can flood up to knee height. Postpone your visit on days with a flood forecast.
Around Independence Day, security is tighter and there may be bag checks or access restrictions.
Around jeepneys and crowded markets, keep your phone and wallet in front and watch for pickpockets.
